FOREWORD
This Indian Standard ( First Revision ) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Environmental Protection Sectional Committee had been approved by the Chemical Division Council. Phenols, defined as hydroxy derivatives of benzene and its condensed nuclii may occur in domestic and industrial wastewaters, natural waters and portable water supplies. Chlorination of such waters may produce odouriferous and objectional ta~tin8 chlorophenols. Phenol removal processes in water treatment include super chlorination, chlorine dioxide or chloramine treatment. ozonation and activated carbon adsorption. This standard supersedes S7 of IS 3025: 1964 'Methods of sampling and test ( physical and chemical) for water used in industry'. In the preparation of this standard, considerable assistance has been derived from Standard Methods for the Examination of Water and Wastewater, 17th edition published by American Public Health Association, Washington (USA). 1989 and EPA�1979 'Methods for Chemical Analysis of Water and Wastewater.' . In reporting the result of a test or analysis made in accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall done in accordance with IS 2 : 1960 -Rules for rounding off numerical values ( revised)'.

1.1 This standard prescribes two spectrophotometric methods for the determination of phenol in natural waters, potable water supplies, domestic and industrial wastewaters. a) 4 Amino antipyrine method without chloroform extraction, and b) 4 Amine-antipyrine method with chloroform extraction.
1.% 1t does not apply to differentiate between various kinds of phenols. 2 REFERENCES The following Indian standards are the necessary adjuncts to this standard: IS No. ita; 7022 � Glossary of terms relating to ( Part 1 ) : .t 973 water, sewage and industrial uen ts, Part 1 7022 Glossary of terms relating to ( Part 2 ) : 1979 water, sewage and industrial ferricyanide to form a coloured antipyrine dye. This dye is kept in aqueous solution and the absorbance is measured at 460 nm, This method is recommended fOI concentrations more than 1 mg/l phenol which does not require chloroform extraction technique.

5.1

IDterre~ces

To eliminate or minimize the interferences, use steam distilled sample. Phenols are distilled from non-volatile impurities. Because the volatilization of phenols is gradual, the distilate volume shall ultimately equal that of the original sample.

S.l.t Preliminary Step of Steam Distillation
5.2.1.1 Measure 500 ml of sample into a beaker. Lower the pH to approximately 4'0 with 8�5 percent phosphoric acid. If the sample was already preserved using phosphoric acid, omit the addition of phosphoric acid again. Transfer to the distillation apparatus made up of glass, consisting of a 1 litre borosilicate glass distilling ~pparatus with Graham condenser. '.1.1.% Distil 450 ml of sample and stop the 4istillation. When boiling ceases, add 50 ml of "arm distilled water to the distilling ftask and tesume distillation until SOO ml have been collected. 5.2.1.3 I f the disti IJate is turbid, filter through a pre-washed membrane filter.

PRESERVATION AND STORAGE

Phenol concentration usually encountered In wastewaters are subject to biological and chel!'ical oxidation. Preserve and store samples at 4-C or lower but do not allow to freeze unless analysed within 4 hours after collection.
